title: Kiddush
hook: a cup of wine or grape juice declares the day holy, remembering creation and the Exodus

segments.voice: Yesterday, a guest at the Friday table: Shabbat shalom at the door, and a quiet moment after washing. Your line was you don't have to know the words. Today, the cup a guest sees lifted first.
screen: `YOU DON'T HAVE TO KNOW THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: At a wedding, someone taps a glass, everyone stands, and a toast turns an ordinary evening into an occasion. Same room, same people. But now it's official: this night matters. On Friday night, in Jewish homes, there's a moment like that at the table. Someone lifts a full cup of wine or grape juice, the room goes quiet, and the words turn a Friday evening into something else.
screen: `SOMEONE TAPS A GLASS.` → `NOW IT'S OFFICIAL.` → `A FULL CUP ON FRIDAY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Kiddush means making holy, from the same root as kadosh, holy. It comes from the commandment, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." The rabbis asked: how do you remember a day? You say so, out loud, over a cup of wine, the drink of celebration. Grape juice works too, and some families use it. If there's no wine at all, the blessing can be said over the challah. On Friday night, Kiddush begins with the last lines of the creation story in Genesis: "And the heaven and the earth were finished, and all the host of them." Then God rested on the seventh day and blessed it. Next comes the blessing over the fruit of the vine, then a longer blessing that names two reasons for the day. Shabbat is a remembrance of creation, the world God made and finished. And it's a reminder of the Exodus, leaving Egypt. Why the Exodus? In Deuteronomy, the Sabbath commandment says: remember that you were a slave in Egypt. Slaves don't get days off. Free people do. So every Friday night, one cup holds two memories: the world was made, and the slaves went free. Customs vary. Some stand, some sit. Some hold the cup in the palm of the hand. Afterward, everyone takes a sip, often from little cups poured from the big one. It's short. But like the toast at a wedding, it says out loud: this time is different.
screen: `KIDDUSH: MAKING HOLY.` · `REMEMBER IT OVER WINE.` · `CREATION, AND LEAVING EGYPT.` · `FREE PEOPLE REST.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE SABBATH DAY, TO KEEP IT HOLY.`

segments.voice: Pick up whatever drink is near you, water or coffee is fine, or picture one. Think of one thing in your life you didn't make but get to enjoy, and one way you're more free than you once were. Lift the cup a little and say one sentence of thanks, out loud if you can, to God if you pray, then drink slowly.
Kiddush. Making holy: a blessing over wine or grape juice that declares Shabbat holy, remembering creation and the Exodus.
Your line: make it holy out loud. You remember a day by saying so. Day one hundred two is in the books.

howItsDone: On Friday night, before the meal, someone at the table lifts a cup of wine or grape juice and recites Kiddush, beginning with Genesis 2:1–3, and everyone then takes a sip.
